section_1.title: Prerequisite & Hook: The 'Same' Vector
section_1.content: Define a vector as a geometric arrow (independent of coordinates). Introduce the idea that while the arrow stays the same, the 'language' (basis) used to describe it can change. Use the analogy of describing a location: '3 miles North, 2 miles East' vs. 'GPS coordinates'.
section_1.example: A cat sitting on a 2D floor. Describe its position relative to the corner of the room (Basis A) versus relative to the center of the rug (Basis B).

section_2.title: Defining Basis Vectors
section_2.content: Explain a basis as a coordinate system defined by linearly independent vectors. Visualize standard basis vectors (e.g., î=[1,0], ĵ=[0,1]) and transform them into custom basis vectors (e.g., b1=[1,1], b2=[-1,1]).
section_2.example: Animation: Show the grid lines stretching and rotating from the standard square grid to a skewed, tilted grid.

section_3.title: The Change-of-Basis Matrix
section_3.content: Introduce the transition matrix (P). Explain that P maps coordinates from the 'New' basis back to the 'Standard' basis. Emphasize the formula: [v]standard = P * [v]new. Show this visually by projecting the new vector components onto the standard axes.
section_3.example: Robot Arm: Mapping the position of a robot's claw from its own 'hand-centric' coordinate system to the 'room-centric' coordinate system.

section_4.title: Step-by-Step Calculation Procedure
section_4.content: Provide a clear 3-step algorithm: 1. Identify the 'New' basis vectors. 2. Construct matrix P by placing basis vectors as columns. 3. Multiply P by the coordinates in the new basis to find the standard representation.
section_4.example: Given Basis B = {[2,1], [1,2]}, convert the coordinate vector [1,1]_B into standard coordinates: 1*[2,1] + 1*[1,2] = [3,3].

section_5.title: Synthesis & Practical Application
section_5.content: Summarize that changing bases allows us to simplify complex problems (like diagonalizing matrices). Highlight that the vector 'object' is invariant; only its 'description' changes.
section_5.example: Video Game Physics: Moving a character 'forward' relative to the camera's current perspective versus the world's fixed north direction.
